task: A centrally switched AP uses one untagged VLAN on its Ethernet link. Wireless client frames travel inside CAPWAP to the controller. Select the switchport mode; the access VLAN is configured separately.

teaching.hint: Follow the frames on this cable, rather than the wireless clients’ eventual VLANs.
teaching.takeaway: An access port is sufficient because only one untagged Ethernet VLAN crosses this AP link. Different client subnets at the controller do not by themselves require a trunk at the AP.

task: This AP now switches client VLAN 20 locally with tags and sends management untagged in VLAN 10. The switch port is already a trunk with both VLANs allowed. Set its native VLAN to match the AP.

teaching.hint: The untagged management frames determine the native VLAN.
teaching.takeaway: The native VLAN maps the untagged management traffic; VLAN 20 remains tagged. A controller-based label alone does not decide these settings—the AP’s actual forwarding and tagging contract does.

task: An AP on SW1 FastEthernet0/1 has an Ethernet link but reports reduced radio operation. On a PoE-capable Cisco switch, display this port’s inline-power state and allocation before changing VLANs.

teaching.hint: Ethernet link state does not establish that the AP received its required power.
teaching.takeaway: Compare allocated power with the AP’s documented requirement and the switch budget. A power display narrows the investigation; it does not independently validate wireless security, registration or client service.
